questions.question: Name the eight planets in order from the Sun. Compare the inner and outer planets in terms of size, composition and surface, giving one feature of a named planet from each group.
questions.expected_answer: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Inner (terrestrial) planets: small, dense, made of rock and metal, solid surfaces, few or no moons, no rings. Outer (giant) planets: much larger, low density, made mainly of hydrogen, helium and ices, no solid surface, many moons, ring systems. Examples: Venus is the hottest planet due to its thick CO₂ atmosphere; Mars is red due to iron oxide dust; Jupiter is the largest planet with the Great Red Spot; Saturn has bright rings and very low density.

questions.question: Define a dwarf planet and name three. Explain why Pluto was reclassified in 2006. Where is the asteroid belt and what are asteroids?
questions.expected_answer: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is massive enough to be nearly round, but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other objects (and is not a moon). Examples: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea, Makemake. Pluto shares its region of space with many other Kuiper Belt objects (e.g. Eris, about the same size), so under the IAU's 2006 definition of a planet it has not cleared its orbit and was reclassified as a dwarf planet. The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter; asteroids are rocky or metallic bodies smaller than planets, leftover material that never formed a planet.

questions.question: Describe the Kuiper Belt and the Oort Cloud. Describe the structure of a comet and explain why its tail points away from the Sun. Distinguish between a meteor and a meteorite.
questions.expected_answer: Kuiper Belt: a doughnut-shaped region beyond Neptune (about 30–50 AU) of small icy bodies, including Pluto; source of short-period comets. Oort Cloud: a vast, thought-to-exist spherical shell of icy bodies far beyond (thousands to about 100 000 AU), source of long-period comets. A comet has an icy nucleus of ice, dust and rock; near the Sun, ice turns to gas forming a glowing coma and long tails (dust and ion tails). The tails point away from the Sun because sunlight pressure and the solar wind push the gas and dust outward from the Sun. A meteor is the streak of light as a meteoroid burns up in the atmosphere; a meteorite is a piece that survives and lands on the ground.
